# Passage classification prompt v0.3.1 — calibrated E

Analyse the highlighted direct or embedded equivalent of “I love you” in the
supplied passage. Return JSON matching `classification_schema_v0_3.json`.

v0.3.1 retains the v0.3 schema and asks the same deliberately narrow question:
how well can the semantic/pragmatic force of the **core utterance** be
represented by T/P/E, with O available to register genuine failure? Literary
context is evidence for that judgement, not a second exhaustive ontology.

## 1. Identify the core event

State briefly which love utterance is being classified and give its
`utterance_status`: `direct`, `quoted_or_revoiced`, `reported`, `imagined`,
`written`, `nonverbal_verbalised`, `hypothetical`, or `other`. Choose the status
that best identifies the event; use its open description for combinations or
important complications. Quotation alone does not imply O: a quoted utterance
may represent an original T, P, or E event.

## 2. Score the compact core ontology

Give four **independent integer support scores from 0 to 4**. They need not sum
to anything, and several may receive substantial support.

- **T — truth-conditional (`truth_conditional`):** the core utterance
  substantially reports, avows, or presents as true a loving emotional or
  mental state.
- **P — performative (`performative`):** the core utterance substantially
  undertakes, enacts, renews, or invokes a commitment, obligation, or
  relational undertaking. Affection, reassurance, courtship, emotional impact,
  or talk of a shared future does not by itself establish P.
- **E — expressive/reflexive (`exclamatory_reflexive`):** the words substantially
  function as an expressive discharge or reflex-like verbal response produced by
  the speaker’s affective state, rather than merely as a passionately delivered
  assertion or undertaking. The schema field retains its v0.3 name for data
  compatibility; “expressive/reflexive” is the narrower human-readable label.
- **O — other (`other`):** there is an important aspect of the core utterance
  itself that no suitable combination of T/P/E adequately represents.

T concerns mode, not truth: a lie can score T=4. P concerns undertaking force,
not whether a commitment is sincere or will be honoured. E concerns presented
expressive/reflexive force, not whether spontaneity is genuine. Deception,
manipulation, and calculation are therefore orthogonal contextual matters.

### E requires independent core force

**Passion is not E.** Do not assign E merely because the utterance is emotional,
emphatic, apparently spontaneous, passionate, sexually charged, shouted,
whispered, gasped, repeated, punctuated as an exclamation, accompanied by crying
or bodily arousal, or otherwise intense. T and P can themselves be expressed
with arbitrarily strong emotion. These features are contextual evidence about
delivery; none by itself establishes expressive/reflexive core force.

Assign E > 0 only when there is positive evidence that producing the words
functions, at least in part, as an expressive or reflex-like discharge **rather
than merely as an emotionally intense realisation of T and/or P**. Ask the
counterfactual diagnostic: would something important about the core utterance be
lost if it were represented using only its T and P scores, plus contextual
information about intensity, prosody, spontaneity, repetition, and delivery? If
not, assign E=0.

E may coexist with T or P when each function has independent support. For
orientation only: T roughly says “I have loving feelings for you”; P roughly says
“I commit myself to you or us”; E roughly says “the emotional state itself
produces the words.” These glosses clarify the contrast but do not replace the
definitions. A genuine expressive/reflexive case belongs under E rather than O.

Calibration contrasts:

- “I LOVE YOU!” screamed through tears can remain high T and E=0 when it is an
  emphatic avowal; typography, tears, and shouting do not supply E.
- “I love you, and I will stay whatever happens” can support P and T without E.
- after months of reflection, finally shouting “I love you!” can remain dominant
  T despite its intensity.
- “He heard himself blurt ‘I love you!’ before he had thought about what he was
  saying” supplies positive evidence for E, perhaps alongside T if independently
  supported.

### O has a deliberately high burden of proof

**Use O if and only if you believe there is an important aspect of the core
utterance itself that cannot be adequately represented by any suitable
combination of T, P and E.**

Do not use O merely because the surrounding context is ambiguous, deceptive,
ironic, quoted, hedged, manipulative, coercive, narratively complex, or
otherwise difficult. If uncertain between T/P/E, express that uncertainty in
their scores, `confidence`, and `ambiguity`; do **not** use O to express doubt.
Even O=1 must indicate genuine residual pressure against T/P/E, not merely a
conceivable alternative.

Plausible O cases include purely instrumental microphone testing, grammar or
pronunciation practice, rote imitation without semantic grounding, use as a
learned social token without ordinary love-related understanding, deliberately
idiosyncratic meaning, or radically nonhuman/underdetermined production. These
are examples, not a taxonomy.

If O > 0, `other_diagnosis` must explain precisely what T/P/E misses and why
the missing property belongs to core force rather than surrounding context. If
O = 0, both diagnosis fields must be null.

Give one confidence value from 0 to 1 for the complete T/P/E/O judgement, a
concise core analysis, and a short ambiguity note when significant. Ambiguity
within T/P/E is not ontology failure.

## 3. Interpret context without classifying all of it

Use `contextual_interpretation` for a concise but informative open account of
whatever helps justify the scores: deception, self-deception, manipulation,
irony, quotation, revoicing, hedging, participant disagreement, narrative
irony, relationships, or framing. Do not force these potentially unlimited
phenomena into fixed categories.

## 4. Make evidence auditable

Use all legitimately available information needed for the best interpretation:

1. `local_text` in the passage;
2. `supplied_metadata`, including bibliographic and location information; and
3. reliable `background_knowledge` of the wider work.

Do not invent events, wording, or plot facts. Mark uncertain memories as such.
Give each important evidence item a unique ID, provenance, quotation or concise
description, the claim it supports, and confidence. Do not present metadata or
remembered paraphrase as passage wording.

Record separately whether background knowledge was used, familiarity,
confidence, and its contribution. If it was used, include at least one evidence
item with `background_knowledge` provenance; if not, use null confidence and
contribution.

## 5. Assess the ontology, but do not proliferate categories

State whether T/P/E/O gives a `natural`, `strained`, or `inadequate` account.
Describe any residual pressure. Name a candidate recurrent missing dimension
only when the case supplies one; do not promote an interesting single O case
to a fifth category. O cases should first accumulate and then be compared
across independent examples.

The objective is controlled simplification: preserve nuance needed to explain
the core judgement, but do not attempt to formalise all the reasons literature
is interesting. Do not perform or propose large-scale reannotation in this
response.

Графу нужно было, чтоб он указал на Ключарева, понимаю! — сказал Пьер.\n\n— Совсем не нужно, — испуганно сказал адъютант. — За Ключаревым и без этого были грешки, за чтó он и сослан. Но дело в том, что граф очень был возмущен. — «Как же ты мог сочинить?» говорит граф. Взял со стола Гамбургскую газету. «Вот она. Ты не сочинил, а перевел и перевел-то скверно, потому что ты и по-французски, дурак, не знаешь». — Чтó же вы думаете? «Нет, говорит, я никаких газет не читал, я сочинил». — «А коли так, то ты изменник, и я тебя предам суду, и тебя повесят.\n\nГовори, от кого получил?» — «Я никаких газет не видал, а сочинил». Так и осталось. Граф и отца призывал: стоит на своем. И отдали под суд, и приговорили, кажется, к каторжной работе. Теперь отец пришел просить за него. Но дрянной мальчишка! Знаете, эдакой купеческий сынишка, франтик, соблазнитель, слушал где-то лекции и уж думает, что ему чорт не брат. Вот это какой молодчик! Нашел мерзавца-живописца...\n\nXI.\n\nВ середине этого нового рассказа Пьера позвали к главнокомандующему.\n\nПьер вошел в кабинет графа Растопчина. Растопчин, сморщившись, потирал лоб и глаза рукой, в то время как вошел Пьер. Но не в том дело. Mon cher, entre nous, вы масон? — сказал граф Растопчин строгим тоном, как будто было что-то дурное в этом, но что он намерен был простить. Вам, я думаю, не безызвестно, что господа Сперанский и Магницкий отправлены куда следует; то же сделано с господином Ключаревым, то же и с другими, которые под видом сооружения храма Соломона старались разрушить храм своего отечества. Вы можете понимать, что на это есть причины и что я не мог бы сослать здешнего почт-директора, ежели бы он не был вредный человек. Теперь мне известно, что вы послали ему свой экипаж для подъема из города и даже, что вы приняли от него бумаги для хранения. Прошу вас прекратить сношения с такими господами как Ключарев и ехать отсюда. Голова иногда кругом идет! — Eh bien, mon cher, qu’est ce que vous faites, vous personnellement?\n\n— Mais rien, — отвечал Пьер, все не поднимая глаз и не изменяя выражения задумчивого лица.\n\nГраф нахмурился.\n\n— Un conseil d’ami, mon cher. Décampez et au plutôt, c’est tout ce que je vous dis. A bon entendeur salut! Прощайте, мой милый. Ах, да, — прокричал он ему из двери, — правда ли, что графиня попалась в лапки des saints pères de la Société de Jésus?\n\nПьер ничего не ответил и, нахмуренный и сердитый, каким его никогда не видали, вышел от Растопчина.\n\n—————\n\nКогда он приехал домой, уже смеркалось. Человек восемь разных людей побывало у него в этот вечер. Секретарь комитета, полковник его батальона, управляющий, дворецкий и разные просители. У всех были дела до Пьера, которые он должен был разрешить. Пьер ничего не понимал, не интересовался этими делами и давал на все вопросы только такие ответы, которые бы освободили его от этих людей. Наконец, оставшись один, он распечатал и прочел письмо жены.\n\n«Они — солдаты на батарее, князь Андрей убит... старик... Простота есть покорность Богу. Страдать надо... значение всего... сопрягать надо... жена идет замуж... Забыть и понять надо...» И он, подойдя к постели, не раздеваясь, повалился на нее и тотчас же заснул.\n\nКогда он проснулся на другой день утром, дворецкий пришел доложить, что от графа Растопчина пришел нарочно посланный полицейский чиновник — узнать, уехал ли или уезжает ли граф Безухов.\n\nЧеловек десять разных людей, имеющих дело до Пьера, ждали его в гостиной. Пьер поспешно оделся и, вместо того чтоб итти к тем, которые ожидали его, он пошел на заднее крыльцо и оттуда вышел в ворота.\n\nС тех пор и до конца московского разорения, никто из домашних Безуховых, несмотря на все поиски, не видал больше Пьера и не знал, где он находился.", "policy": "radius_3000_expanded_outward_to_paragraph_boundaries"}}, "TRANSLATION_ANALYTICAL_AID": {"status": "provided", "text": "“You see,” the adjutant was saying, “it is a tangled story. This proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed. He ordered an investigation. So Gavrilo Ivanych made inquiries: this proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three pairs of hands. He would go to one man: ‘Whom did you get it from?’—‘So-and-so.’ He would go to that man: ‘Whom did you get it from?’ and so on, until they reached Vereshchagin... a half-educated young merchant, you know, a dear little merchant,” the adjutant said with a smile. “They ask him: ‘Whom did you get it from?’ And the main thing is that we know whom he got it from. He could have got it from no one but the postmaster. But there had evidently been some collusion between them. He says: ‘From no one; I wrote it myself.’ They threatened and entreated him, but he stood by it: ‘I wrote it myself.’ That was how it was reported to the count. The count ordered him to be summoned. ‘Whom did you get the proclamation from?’—‘I wrote it myself.’ Well, you know the count!” the adjutant said with a proud and cheerful smile. “He flew into a terrible rage, and just think of it: such insolence, lying, and obstinacy!...\n\n“Ah! The count wanted him to implicate Klyucharev, I understand!” said Pierre.\n\n“Not at all,” the adjutant said in alarm. “There were sins enough against Klyucharev even without that, and that is why he was exiled. But the point is that the count was extremely indignant. ‘How could you have written it?’ says the count. He took the Hamburg newspaper from the table. ‘Here it is. You did not write it; you translated it, and translated it badly at that, because, fool that you are, you do not even know French.’ Well, what do you think? ‘No,’ he says, ‘I have not read any newspapers; I wrote it myself.’—‘And if that is so, then you are a traitor, and I shall have you brought to trial, and you will be hanged.\n\n“‘Tell me, whom did you receive it from?’—‘I have not seen any newspapers; I wrote it myself.’ And that is how the matter remained. The count summoned his father too, but he stood his ground. And they put him on trial and sentenced him, I think, to hard labor. Now his father has come to plead for him. But he is a worthless brat! You know the sort: a merchant’s little son, a fop and seducer, who attended some lectures somewhere and now thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That is the kind of fine fellow he is! His father has a tavern here by the Stone Bridge, and in the tavern, you know, there is a large icon of God Almighty, depicted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other; well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what do you think he did? He found a scoundrel of a painter...\n\nXI.\n\nIn the middle of this new story, Pierre was summoned to the commander in chief.\n\nPierre entered Count Rastopchin’s study. Rastopchin was frowning and rubbing his forehead and eyes with his hand as Pierre entered. A short man was saying something and, as soon as Pierre came in, fell silent and left.\n\n“Ah! Good day, great warrior,” said Rastopchin as soon as the man had left. “I have heard about your feats! But that is not the point. My dear fellow, between ourselves, are you a Freemason?” Count Rastopchin said in a stern tone, as though there were something bad in that, but something he intended to forgive. Pierre was silent. “My dear fellow, I am well informed, but I know that there are Masons and Masons, and I hope you do not belong to those who, under the guise of saving the human race, wish to destroy Russia.”\n\n“Yes, I am a Freemason,” Pierre replied.\n\n“Well then, you see, my dear fellow. I think you are not unaware that Messrs. Speransky and Magnitsky have been sent where they belong; the same has been done with Mr. Klyucharev, and likewise with others who, under the guise of building the temple of Solomon, sought to destroy the temple of their fatherland. You can understand that there are reasons for this and that I could not have exiled the local postmaster if he had not been a dangerous man. I now know that you sent him your carriage to take him out of the city and even that you accepted papers from him for safekeeping. I love you and wish you no harm, and since you are half my age, I advise you, as a father, to break off all relations with people of that sort and to leave here yourself as soon as possible.”\n\n“But what is Klyucharev guilty of, Count?” Pierre asked.\n\n“That is for me to know and not for you to ask me,” Rastopchin shouted.\n\n“If he is accused of circulating Napoleon’s proclamations, that has not been proved,” said Pierre, without looking at Rastopchin, “and Vereshchagin...”\n\n“There we are,” Rastopchin suddenly shouted, frowning, interrupting Pierre, and raising his voice even louder than before. “Vereshchagin is a traitor and a betrayer who will receive the punishment he deserves,” Rastopchin said with the heat of malice with which people speak when recalling an insult. “But I did not summon you to discuss my affairs, but to give you advice—or an order, if that is what you want. I ask you to break off relations with gentlemen such as Klyucharev and to leave this place. And I shall knock the foolishness out of anyone, whoever he may be.” And, probably realizing that he seemed to be shouting at Bezukhov, who had not yet been guilty of anything, he added, taking Pierre amicably by the hand: “We are on the eve of a public disaster, and I have no time to say pleasant things to everyone who has business with me. Sometimes my head is in a whirl! Well then, my dear fellow, what are you doing, you personally?”\n\n“Why, nothing,” Pierre replied, still without raising his eyes or changing the thoughtful expression on his face.\n\nThe count frowned.\n\n“A friend’s advice, my dear fellow. Clear out, and as soon as possible; that is all I have to say to you. A word to the wise is enough! Good-bye, my dear fellow. Oh, yes,” he called after him from the doorway, “is it true that the countess has fallen into the clutches of the holy fathers of the Society of Jesus?”\n\nPierre did not answer and, frowning and angry as no one had ever seen him, left Rastopchin.\n\n—————\n\nBy the time he arrived home, dusk was already falling. About eight different people came to see him that evening: the committee secretary, the colonel of his battalion, his steward, his butler, and various petitioners. They all had matters requiring Pierre’s attention that he had to settle. Pierre understood nothing, took no interest in these matters, and gave only such answers to all their questions as would rid him of these people. At last, when he was alone, he unsealed and read his wife’s letter.\n\n“They are soldiers at the battery, Prince Andrei has been killed... the old man... Simplicity is submission to God.
